The minutes of the previous
meeting held on 04 August 2026 were APPROVED as a correct
record and SIGNED by the Leader.

The
Cabinet had before it, and NOTED, the notification of Key Decisions
*.

 

The
Clerk stated that no additional items had been added to the Forward Plan since
it was published as part of the agenda pack for the meeting.

 

Note: * Key Decisions previously circulated.

The
Cabinet had before it a report * from the Deputy Chief Executive (S151) on the
2027/28 Budget update.

 

The
Cabinet Member for Governance, Finance and Risk outlined the contents of the
report with particular reference to the
following:

 

·       The report provided an important and constructive
update on the development of the Council’s 2027-28 budget.

·       Although the financial outlook remained challenging,
significant work had already been undertaken to identify practical options for
both the General Fund (GF) and the Housing Revenue Account (HRA). 

·       The proposed approach showed a potential route to
balancing the GF while also making meaningful progress in reducing the HRA
shortfall.

·       It was to be noted that this was at an early stage of
the budget process and the position would continue to
evolve as assumptions were refined. 

·       The report therefore sought Cabinet support for the
proposed approach and invited the Policy Development Groups to help identify
further deliverable savings, ensuring Members played a full role in shaping a
balanced, sustainable budget that protected the Council’s priorities and
essential services.

 

Discussion
took place with regards to:

 

·      
Section 3.2.1 of
the report which mentioned a possible reduction in the contribution to
Earmarked Reserves. It was explained that, in the past, significant amounts had
been put into various Earmarked Reserves to fund future asset maintenance and replacements,
however, in order to close the budget gap, it may be
necessary to reduce these contributions. Further review work would take place
after the Policy Development Groups had met in September.

·      
It was confirmed
that sufficient resources would be made available to fund Planning Enforcement.
The department now had the full complement of staff having undergone a recent
review of this area. The Planning Enforcement team were one of the most robust
in the county. The team had to deal with a significant number of cases in a
rolling programme. Much of this data needed to be protected, therefore, if a Member had a query they were encouraged to contact the team
directly.

 

RESOLVED that:

 

1.    
The proposed
approach to balancing the 2027/28 General Fund and Housing Revenue Account
budget gaps be APPROVED. 

2.    
The Policy Development
Groups be requested to identify and recommend further deliverable savings
options to Cabinet.

 

(Proposed
by Cllr J Downes and seconded by Cllr J Lock)

 

 

Reason
for decision:

 

By
undertaking regular reviews of the MTFP the Council could ensure that its
Corporate Plan priorities were affordable. The implications of the budget gap
were set out within the paper. Therefore, a number of
key assumptions underpinned the reported position, which would be refined as
greater clarity was received through the budget setting process. 

 

Note: * Report previously circulated.

The
Cabinet had before it a report * from the Director of Place and Economy for
approval for the East Cullompton Strategic Design Code to go out for public
consultation. 

 

As
items 6 and 7 on the agenda were closely linked and complimentary, the Cabinet
Member for Planning, Economic and Regeneration outlined the contents of both
reports with particular reference to the
following:

 

Strategic
Design Code

 

a)   
The Council had
commissioned a design company to prepare a Strategic Design Code for East Cullompton
which was allocated through policies CU7-CU12 of the Mid Devon Local Plan.  

 

b)   
The Code added
detail to the adopted Masterplan Supplementary Planning Document (SPD) and
would be used to guide design aspects of the development of East
Cullompton.  It was intended to be for a
wide audience including planners, developers, designers, the local community
and Town and Parish Councils.  Outline
and detailed planning applications would be expected to comply with the
Strategic Design Code.

 

c)    
The Design Code
developed the vision set out in the Masterplan SPD, defining the intended look,
feel and character of the place.  It
provided key Structuring Principles and detailed Codes to ensure that the most
important elements of the masterplan were fixed without stifling innovation and
creativity during the detailed design stage. 


 

d)   
The Code covered
strategically important parts of the site, with its purpose being to ensure a
consistent and co-ordinated approach to design and delivery.  Detailed Codes were set out under four
Frameworks: placemaking, activity, landscape and mobility.

 

e)   
The Strategic
Design Code was presented to the Planning Policy Advisory Group (PPAG) on 28
July 2026 and had been well received. 
PPAG had the following comments and recommendations to make:

 

·      
Consideration
should be given to the name of the garden village.  Residents would prefer ‘Cullompton Garden
Village’, rather than ‘Culm Garden Village’. 


·      
Concern that
‘Moorhayes’ village could be confused with Moorhayes in Tiverton, and that
‘Hayes Moor’ would be more appropriate.

·      
Faith space
should be explicitly mentioned.

·      
The document
should mention places to sit in the shade.

·      
Park run should
be explicitly mentioned.

 

f)     
These
recommendations would be added to feedback from the public engagement.

 

g)   
The Strategic
Design Code was presented to the Planning, Environment and Sustainability
Policy Development Group on 3 August 2026. 
A recommendation was made to add a public exhibition to the
consultation, and it was agreed that officers would attend Cullompton Autumn
Fest on 10 October 2026 to facilitate this.

 

h)   
Subject to
Cabinet approval, it was proposed that a public consultation takes place over a
4-week period in September and October 2026 (dates to be finalised).

 

i)      
The consultation
was proposed to include:

 

·      
Consultation with
technical consultees.

·      
Public engagement
through Let’s Talk Mid Devon.

·      
Publication of
the draft document on the Culm Garden Village website.

·      
Presentations to Cullompton
Town Council and Kentisbeare Parish Council that the public can attend.

·      
An exhibition stand at Cullompton Autumn Fest.

 

j)      
Feedback from the
public consultation would help to shape the final version of the Strategic
Design Code.

 

Discussion
took place with regards to:

 

·      
The provision of
self-build properties and the process for reallocating s106 contributions where
self-builds do not come forward and are replaced with market housing.  The infrastructure requirements would not
change should self-build be replaced with market housing.

·      
The importance of
the Stewardship Working Group in developing community stewardship proposals and
the need to build up mutual trust between all participants.

·      
Cullompton Town
Council were playing an active role in stewardship discussions.

·      
The Biodiversity
Net Gain (BNG) percentage required and how BNG is built into the need to
alleviate flood risk? It was confirmed that this was a high priority as could
be evidenced by the name ‘Garden Village’. Much background work has been done
to ensure that biodiversity considerations are integral to the design, which is
landscape-led. The 10% BNG requirement is a statutory one and the design code
cannot introduce new policy by setting higher targets.

·      
Similar
to the NBG requirements
considerations regarding solar panels and wind turbines are set out in planning
policy and would come through via planning applications. However, the team would
continue to work closely with developers on the climate and ecological
emergencies.

·      
Provisions for
fire suppression would be dealt with through Building Regulations.

·      
Concerns were
expressed that the consultation exercise would become little more than a
‘process’, however, it needed to demonstrate that comments made would be
reflected in the final proposals coming forward for approval. Participation in
the consultation needed to be maximised wherever possible not just online formats
but also ‘face to face’ engagement. There was also concern four weeks was not
long enough for a consultation and it must be actively promoted throughout this
period through as many channels as possible. People’s voices needed to be
genuinely heard and factored into the resulting document. It was confirmed that
this absolutely was the intention and that the Council would listen to all
comments.  

 

RESOLVED that the East Cullompton Strategic Design Code
be NOTED and APPROVED for public consultation

 

(Proposed
by Cllr S Keable and seconded by Cllr L Knight)

 

Reason
for decision:

 

The
Strategic Design Code would provide guidance on the planning and delivery of a
strategic site for Mid Devon. The Strategic Design Code directly related to all
five aims of the Corporate Plan 2024-28: Planning, Environment &
Sustainability, Community, People and Equalities, Homes, Economy & Assets
and Providing high quality and efficient services to support and improve the
lives of people in Mid Devon.

 

Note: * Report previously circulated.

The
Cabinet had before it a report * from the Director of Place and Economy for
approval for the East Cullompton Phasing and Delivery Strategy to go out for
public consultation. 

 

The
Cabinet Member for Planning, Economic and Regeneration outlined the contents of
the report with particular reference to the
following:

 

Phasing
& Delivery Strategy

 

a)   
The Council had
commissioned Hyas Associates to prepare a Phasing and Delivery Strategy for the
East Cullompton allocation.

 

b)   
The purpose of
the Phasing and Delivery Strategy was to set out how East Cullompton should be
planned, phased and delivered as a coordinated, high-quality extension to
Cullompton.

 

c)    
It translated the
vision and principles in the adopted Masterplan Supplementary Planning Document
(SPD) and draft Strategic Design Code into a practical delivery framework for
landowners, developers, infrastructure providers and decision-makers. Its purpose
was to ensure that development came forward in a way that created a genuinely
walkable, well-connected and characterful place from the outset.

 

d)   
The Strategy was
intended to guide both planning decisions and delivery over time. Planning
applications were expected to demonstrate how they complied with the relevant
phase requirements, how they contributed to the wider development strategy and
how they supported long-term stewardship.

 

e)   
The Strategy was
structured around three principal stages of delivery:

 

·       Phase 1A, Creating East Cullompton, covered the first 500
homes and focussed on establishing the foundations of a new community.  The 500 homes figure was based on the initial
capacity of J28, before J28A was needed.

·       Phase 1B, Establishing East Cullompton, covered
501–1,700 homes and was intended to broaden the range of services and support a
more self-sufficient community.  This
phase would deliver the number of homes allocated within the Local Plan period.

·       Subsequent phases, Completing East Cullompton, covered
the remainder of the allocation and focussed on completing key infrastructure
networks and enabling East Cullompton to function as a fully integrated part of
the wider Garden Village.

 

f)     
Across all
phases, the Strategy identified the infrastructure required to support growth
and placemaking outcomes.  Section 3 of
the Strategy sets out infrastructure delivery in a series of tables.  These linked infrastructure requirements to
triggers, delivery mechanisms, relevant policies and wider spatial guidance in the
Masterplan SPD and Strategic Design Code.

 

g)   
Finally, the
Strategy set out objectives and principles for long-term community stewardship
of public spaces, community assets and other community infrastructure that
would require effective governance, funding and management over time. 

 

h)   
The Phasing and
Delivery Strategy was presented to Planning Policy Advisory Group (PPAG) on 28
July 2026.  No alterations were
recommended at this meeting.

 

i)      
The Phasing and Delivery
Strategy was presented to Planning, Environment and Sustainability Policy
Development Group on 3 August 2026.  A
recommendation was made to add a public exhibition to the consultation
and it was agreed that officers would attend Cullompton Autumn Fest on 10
October 2026 to facilitate this.

 

j)      
Subject to
Cabinet approval, it was proposed that a public consultation on the Phasing and
Delivery Strategy takes place at the same time and in the same way as for the
Strategic Design Code.

 

Discussion
regarding the Phasing and Delivery Strategy had taken place under the previous
item.

  

RESOLVED that the East Cullompton Phasing and Delivery
Strategy be NOTED and APPROVED for public consultation.

 

(Proposed
by Cllr S Keable and seconded by Cllr L Knight)

 

Reason
for decision:

 

The
Phasing and Delivery Strategy would provide guidance on the planning and
delivery of a strategic site for Mid Devon. The Phasing and Delivery Strategy directly
related to all five aims of the Corporate Plan 2024-28: Planning, Environment
& Sustainability, Community, People and Equalities, Homes, Economy &
Assets and Providing high quality and efficient services to support and improve
the lives of people in Mid Devon.

 

Note: * Report previously circulated.

The minutes of the previous
meeting held on 07 July 2026 were APPROVED as a correct record
and SIGNED by the Leader.

from voting as was not present at the last meeting.

purpose:
Acquisition of freehold
employment land at Tiverton EUE for new housing depot.
content:
Acquisition of freehold
employment land at Tiverton EUE for new housing depot.



As per the
approved, adopted Housing Revenue Account budget for 2026/27 and Medium-Term
Financial Plan, the acquisition of employment land to provide a new,
replacement Mid Devon Housing (MDH) depot and offices to replace the current
Old Road Depot.

 

Old Road
Depot

Old Road is
an end-of-life asset which has operated as the base for the building services
element of Mid Devon Housing for many years. It was never purpose designed as a
housing depot, having been originally constructed post-war as a bus depot.

The property
is old, structurally poor and would require significant (non-viable) levels of
investment to operate as a modern, safe housing depot in the future.

Since early
2025, the upper floor of the depot has been closed, principally for safety
reasons, resulting in the relocation of office-based staff into Phoenix House
alongside tenancy colleagues, leaving the front-line depot, building
maintenance, workshop and stores functions dislocated from the wider service. This
has restricted the ability of the MDH to provide a single, coherent service to
our tenants and created several operational challenges and risks.

Furthermore,
the depot has inadequate parking provision for operational vehicles where space
constraints also create conflict of movement between goods/operational vehicles
and people with resultant safety risk. There is no staff parking and is
external areas of the property are difficult to make secure. The building has
an insufficient electricity supply to support EV charging and IT connections
are limited.

In
accordance with this, Council approved the Housing Revenue Account (HRA) 26/27
budget and Medium-Term Financial Plan with the inclusion of £3m project
approval for a new depot. This includes £1m in 26/27 for land acquisition and
design/planning costs with the remainder of the project budget for build and
commissioning, phased over 26/27 and 27/28.

 

New Depot

Since 2025, the service and an appointed specialist commercial land
agent have been working on behalf of MDH to identify and move forward with the
acquisition of an appropriate commercial land site upon which a new depot can
be built. 

A plot has now been identified on the designated commercial land site
within the Tiverton Eastern Urban Extension that fully meets the essential
criteria for the new depot:

 


 Located within Tiverton (staff retention
     and proximity to largest concentration of council housing)
 Fully serviced plot – ready to build
     site with road access, drainage, power and communication links provided
 Minimum 1 acre plot (1.5
     acre plot is available – sufficient to provide a 6500m2 depot
     building with adequate external area for parking and operational delivery)
 Outline planning permission in place for
     relevant commercial use


 

The site can be identified as Plot D on the attached plan. It is located
immediately south of the A361 Link Road / north of Blundell’s Rd and is a new
business park development (recently named Milestone Business Park) accessed via
Barberry Way.

The vendor is the Chettiscombe Trust and the
plot will be acquired as a freehold with vacant possession. The property will
be granted access rights to any access roads and/or services until which time
as the roads and relevant services will be adopted.

The depot building will be subject to a pre-application and planning
process where the building will be designed to deliver a fully compliant,
modern depot, stores, office, reception and interview/meeting rooms together
with sufficient staff/visitor parking, dedicated goods delivery, fuel storage
and EV charging. The building size and plot will provide for 15-20% additional
space for future expansion of operational capacity if required.

Following identification of the plot, several key elements have been
progressed and are in place to enable a decision to be made on the acquisition
of the land:

 


 Price agreed in principle. The
     acquisition price is currently commercially sensitive but is well within
     the approved acquisition budget
 Independent market valuation completed
     that confirms the land value in line with the proposed acquisition price
     (commercial RICS valuation from a major SW based property specialist)
 Approved draft Heads of Terms – agreed
     between the Council’s legal services and the vendors
 The vendors have progressed reserved
     matters planning application 26/00259/MARM to enable, amongst other
     things, the provision of relevant infrastructure including the access road


 

Next steps and timeline

 

This decision will enable the legal teams on both sides to be formally
instructed to proceed with the acquisition under the Heads of Terms. The plot
will be marked as ‘under offer’ by the vendors marketing agent.

In order to complete the transaction, further to this decision, the
Council is required to obtain planning permission for the erection of the
depot, the seller must construct the relevant infrastructure in accordance with
26/00259/MARM and the seller must obtain subsequent planning permission for an
additional, short access road to serve Plot D (together with adjacent Plots C
and E). The seller must also lay services to Plot D in accordance with an
approved specification.

 

Following exchange of contracts:

 


 The Council have 4-months to submit the
     relevant planning application for the depot building
 Within in six-months of obtaining
     planning consent, the Council must commence construction


 

It is estimated that this will result in commencement of construction in
early autumn 2027. This will enable the seller to bring forward the required
infrastructure including the access road. In accordance with the Heads of
Terms, build must be completed within 12-months following commencement, however
as commercial, steel frame building, its is
anticipated build completion may be possible earlier.

Once detailed design and build specifications are in place, officers
will enter into a tender procurement process to award
the build contract, the decision on which will come to the relevant future
Cabinet meeting in due course, no later than March 2027.

Old Road site remains with Council ownership with potential to redevelop
the vacant site for social housing within MDH stock. This will be subject to a
separate decision.

content:
Development Management
consultation upon updated planning application validation checklist to include
an AI declaration.



The local validation checklist
should be reviewed and republished as required under the Town and Country
Planning (Development Management Procedure) (England) Order 2015 (as amended)
Part 3, Article 11 (3) (d). This requires a review every 2 years. The MDDC
Validation Guidance Note was last updated in September 2025, however that
review did not include provisions for dealing with Artificial Intelligence (AI)
when used to support the submission of planning proposals. Prior to adoption the
planning authority should publish the draft document for public comment.
topline: The Director of Place and Economy has decided to update the planning application validation checklist to include an AI declaration.

content:
Cabinet
had before it a report * from the Corporate Performance and Improvement Manager
and the Head of People, Performance & Waste on the Annual Performance for
2025/2026.

 

The
Leader of the Council outlined the contents of the report with particular reference to the following: 

 


 The Annual Performance
     Report reviewed performance against the Corporate Plan, highlighting
     achievements and areas for improvement. 
 The Council delivered
     strong performance across services despite financial and operational
     challenges. 
 Planning performance
     remained strong, with progress made on Plan Mid Devon, biodiversity net
     gain, and enforcement activities. 
 Commitment to climate
     change and sustainability was demonstrated through EV charging points,
     green grants, biodiversity projects, and other practical initiatives. 
 External funding of
     £472,000 was secured for community carbon reduction projects, nearly five
     times the target. 
 Recognition was given
     to Town and Parish Councils, housing support services, voluntary
     organisations, and resident engagement initiatives. 
 These partnerships and
     services were acknowledged as having a significant positive impact on
     residents. 
 Housing remained a key
     challenge, with investment in existing homes, delivery of new homes, and
     support for homeless applicants continuing. 
 Progress was not
     always as rapid as desired, but the Council maintained a strong commitment
     to housing delivery. 
 A net gain of 75
     homes, including 36 net-zero homes, was achieved. 
 The 550 priority
     applicants on Devon Home Choice highlighted ongoing housing need and the
     importance of continued investment in affordable housing. 
 Continued support was
     provided to local businesses, town centres, the Tiverton Work Hub, Visit
     Mid Devon, and major infrastructure projects. 
 The Council supported
     270 businesses through non-financial assistance during the previous year. 
 This support was
     provided voluntarily to help sustain small businesses in rural
     communities. 
 Thanks were expressed
     to officers and frontline teams, particularly in Waste and Recycling,
     Revenues, and Leisure Services. 
 Strong service
     performance was attributed to staff efforts and residents’ positive
     engagement with Council services. 
 Members were referred
     to Appendices 1–5 for detailed information on Corporate Plan objectives.


 

Discussion
took place with regards to:

 


 Clarification
     regarding the Voluntary, Community, and Social Enterprise (VSCE) sector
     and the information provided in the report. It was explained that, while
     the Council remained committed to supporting organisations through its
     grant schemes, funding available to the VCSE sector was reducing due to
     the ending of larger programmes such as the UK Shared Prosperity Fund. It
     was clarified that this reflected a decrease in available funding streams
     rather than any reduction in the Council’s commitment to supporting the
     sector.



 Members acknowledged
     the process that the Council had shown through the performance report and
     asked for a press release to be published via the Communication Team.  
 That the resident
     survey in relation to how the Council ran services had remained broadly
     consistent with the previous year. Concerns was
     expressed that satisfaction levels remained below the Council’s 70%
     target, and it was suggested that there should be greater promotion of the
     Council’s achievements through the residents’ app, social media and other
     communication channels to help improve public awareness and increase
     satisfaction levels.


 

RESOLVED that:

 


 Cabinet reviewed and
     scrutinised the performance indicators and information detailed in the
     report.
 Consideration to the
     proposed changes to performance indicators outlined in section 3 of the
     report were APPROVED.


 

(Proposed
by the Leader)

 

Reason
for Decision:

Corporate
Plan priorities and targets were managed and scrutinised on a regular basis
using appropriate performance indicators as detailed in the report.

 

Note:
*Report previously circulated
topline: The Cabinet approves recommendations in the Annual Performance Report, addressing achievements and areas for improvement in services.

content:
Cabinet
had before it and NOTED a report * from the Corporate Performance and
Improvement Manager and the Head of People, Performance & Waste on the
Corporate Risk Report.

 

The
Leader of the Council outlined the contents of the report with particular reference to the following: 

 


 It was reported that there were
     currently 12 risks on the Corporate Risk Register relating to the delivery
     of the Corporate Plan. 
 It was noted that, although no other
     risk ratings had changed since the previous update, risk owners had
     reviewed and updated risk descriptions and mitigation actions to ensure
     they remained accurate and current. 
 Three risks had been de-escalated from
     the Corporate Risk Register and would now be managed at service level,
     demonstrating active management of the register. 
 It was emphasised that risks no longer
     requiring corporate oversight were being managed through appropriate
     service arrangements. 


 

The
Corporate Performance and Improvement Manager advised Members that the
Corporate Risk Register was reviewed quarterly by risk owners, the Corporate
Management Team and the Leadership Team. A correction was made to confirm that
the risk rating for CR1A (Culm Garden Village capacity funding) should have
been 15 rather than nine, with the discrepancy attributed to an administrative
error and the evolving nature of the risk assessment process, as the final
rating had only been agreed towards the end of the review period. 

 

Discussion
took place with regards to:

 


 A concern was raised that the
     description of Risk CR19, which carried a current risk rating of 20, was
     not clearly articulated and appeared to describe the situation rather than
     the potential impact of the risk. It was suggested that the mitigating
     actions did not adequately reflect the Council’s engagement with residents
     and that this should be included as a mitigation measure. It was agreed
     that the comments would be considered as part of a further review of the
     risk with the Chief Executive. It was noted that, as decisions on Local
     Government Reorganisation progressed, the Council would need to define and
     manage the associated risks more clearly, potentially through a dedicated
     risk register similar to those being developed by
     other councils.


 

Note:
*Report previously circulated
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve recommendations from the Corporate Risk Report, addressing risks related to the delivery of the Corporate Plan.

Cabinet
had before it a report * from the Strategic Manager for Growth, Economy &
Delivery seeking approval for the continuation of shopfront enhancements for
the districts three main towns with seed funding of £24,000 and that the level
of grant offered be increased from 50% to 70%.

 

The
Cabinet Member for Planning and Economic Regeneration outlined the contents of
the report with particular reference to the
following: 

 


 It was reported that
     the grant scheme had operated successfully for several years, providing
     property owners and shopkeepers with funding for minor repairs and
     improvements to shopfronts. 
 Approximately 10
     properties per year had benefited from the scheme, contributing to the
     upkeep and visual appeal of the district’s high streets and town centres. 
 It was noted that the
     scheme had closed in each of the district’s three towns.
 The Economy and Assets
     Policy Development Group (PDG) had supported the continuation of the
     initiative and proposed reopening the schemes. 
 It was recognised that
     retailers were facing challenging economic conditions and often struggled
     to invest in property maintenance. 
 The PDG had proposed
     increasing the grant contribution from 50% to 70% to enable more
     businesses to access the scheme and improve their premises.


 

Discussion
took with regards to:

 


 Whether the proposed
     £24,000 funding allocation would be sufficient to make a meaningful impact
     on supporting high streets, given the significant pressures facing town
     centre businesses? It was explained that the proposed funding reflected
     previous levels of investment and had historically been successful in
     attracting additional funding. While demand could vary, it was considered
     sufficient to support the scheme and was expected to provide funding for
     approximately the next two years.
 It was noted that some
     shopkeepers had previously found the requirement to obtain three quotes
     had been a barrier to accessing the scheme.
 It was suggested that
     greater promotion of the more flexible approach now being taken could help
     increase participation in the grant scheme.
 Cullompton appeared to
     have a higher-than-average vacancy rate, and a question was raised as to
     whether the grant scheme created opportunities to engage with property
     owners. It was explained that yes this was already underway.
 It was suggested that
     these conversations could help the Council explore additional ways to
     encourage the occupation and rental of vacant properties, beyond improving
     shopfronts.


 

RESOLVED that:

 


 Approval was given for
     the continuation of shopfront enhancement schemes for each of the three
     main market towns in the district with seed fund totalling £24,000.


 


 The level of grant
     offered by the scheme to increase from 50% to 70%.


 

As recommended by the Economy Policy Development
Group.

 

(Proposed
by Cllr S Keable and seconded by Cllr G DuChesne)

 

Reason
for Decision:

The
Shopfront Enhancement Scheme supported the corporate priority for economy and
assets, in particular: ‘regenerating our town centres’.

  

Note:
*Report previously circulated
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve the continuation of shopfront enhancement schemes for the district's main towns with increased funding and grant contribution.

content:
Cabinet
had before it a report * from the Head of People, Performance & Waste and
the Operations Manager for Street Scene and Open Spaces providing information
regarding proposals to stimulate greater resident awareness and participation
with the Bin-It 123 scheme and a review of potential additional recycling
material collections that would be a priority including an implementation
timetable.

 

The Cabinet Member for Service Delivery and Continuous Improvement
outlined the contents of the report with particular reference
to the following: 

 


 A 12‑month waste
     service implementation plan had been developed, including pilot
     collections, new recycling containers, resident awareness campaigns and
     increased capacity ahead of the Christmas period. 
 The service had
     achieved 5% recycling performance in 2024/25, generating approximately £3
     million in income and a projected £1.41 million Extended Producer
     Responsibility (EPR) payment. 
 Members were advised
     that further improvements in recycling could generate an additional
     £660,000 for reinvestment in frontline services. 
 Work had been undertaken
     with schools, communities and Councillors to promote recycling and improve
     access to food caddies and recycling containers. 
 A food waste education
     and enforcement campaign had commenced to increase recycling rates and
     improve compliance. 
 Progress had been made
     on the depot reconfiguration, including improved facilities, increased
     recycling capacity and site enhancements. 
 Approval was sought
     for additional capital investment of approximately £1 million to replace
     the recycling sort line, funded in part through EPR funding. 
 It was noted that
     failure to replace the sort line would increase health and safety risks
     and could result in the loss of around £175,000 in annual income. 
 It was emphasised that
     the investment would support the Council’s position as a leader in
     recycling and strengthen future waste service provision.


 

Discussion took place with regards to:


 Appreciation was expressed for the clear
     presentation of the timeline, charts and figures within the report and
     noted that around 3,000 tonnes of food waste continued to be disposed of
     in black bins, representing approximately 25% of residual waste.
 A concern was raised that the use of
     intervention stickers should take into account
     which residents compost or produce very little food waste.
 It was suggested that the accompanying
     communications campaign should emphasise that the stickers formed part of
     an educational initiative to encourage recycling, rather than being
     perceived as a punitive measure.
 Whether the site visit included Bonster the food monster.- It
     was confirmed that this was correct.
 A question was raised regarding the
     significant increase in the estimated cost of replacing the sort line,
     from approximately £150,000 to around £1 million. It was explained that the cost of
     materials had increased over the years. The new sort line was considered
     essential for the effective separation of recyclable materials and for
     supporting future recycling initiatives, including soft plastics
     collection. 
 Clarification was sought on the reasons
     for the increased investment requirement and the need for replacement,
     given that the existing sort line had been identified as being at the end
     of its economic life. It was explained that the existing sort line had
     been in operation for approximately 13–15 years and had been transferred
     from the previous depot.
 Whether the plastic sack for the soft
     plastic collection was a single use sack or reuseable. It was confirmed it
     was reuseable. 


 

RESOLVED that:

 


 The implementation
     timetable regarding future proposals and reforms related to the Bin-It 123
     scheme was NOTED and APPROVED.


 


 Cabinet supported the
     steps detailed in this paper to reinvigorate resident focus on recycling
     and the upcoming enforcement activity regarding food waste. 


 


 Cabinet approves and
     recommends to Full Council an increase in the Capital Programme of up to
     £1,000,000 to purchase a replacement sort line for its recycling materials
     and allows for a permanent collection of soft plastics (flexibles) in
     April 2027. 


 

As
recommended by the Service Delivery and Continuous Improvement Policy 

Development
Group.  

 

(Proposed
by Cllr J Wright and seconded by Cllr Steve Keable)

 

Reason
for Decision:

This
report identifies within the Corporate Plan for 2024-2028, and in particular 5.2 – We will increase our
recycling services, enabling our communities to achieve even higher levels of
recycling. Supporting and enabling customers to recycle and reduce
residual waste contributes to the Council’s commitment to the Devon Climate
Emergency.

 

Note:
*Report previously circulated
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve recommendations to enhance recycling initiatives and invest in a replacement sort line for recycling materials.

Cabinet
had before it and NOTED a report * from the Head of Revenues, Benefits
and Leisure and the Revenues and Benefits Operations Manager to provide an
overview of the local delivery of the Crisis and Resilience Fund (CaRF), including Crisis Payments, Resilience Services,
Housing Payments and Heating Oil Support.

 

The
Cabinet Member for Governance, Finance and Risk outlined the contents of the
report with particular reference to the
following: 

 


 This report outlined the delivery of the
     Crisis and Resilience Fund (CaRF), a
     government-funded scheme introduced from 1 April 2026 to replace the
     Housing Support Fund and bring together crisis support, housing assistance
     and financial resilience services into a single framework. 
 Delivery operated through a Devon-wide
     partnership, with Devon County Council overseeing governance and Mid Devon
     delivering local support alongside partners CHAT and Navigate. 
 The scheme provided:


Ø  Immediate Crisis Payments for households in
financial hardship- Funding £335,419.

Ø  Resilience support to reduce repeat crises- Funding
£159,453.

Ø  Housing Payments (previously known as Discretionary
Housing Payments)- Funding £77,202.

Ø  Heating Oil Support scheme for low-income
households - Funding £132,630.

Ø  Total Government funding for Mid Devon in 2026/27
was £704,704


 The scheme supported vulnerable
     residents, aligned with the Council’s Corporate Plan priorities, and would
     be closely monitored and reported to ensure effective delivery and
     compliance with DWP requirements, this new approach also has Ministerial
     oversight.


 

Discussion took place with regards to:

 


 A question was raised as to whether the
     funding scheme could be extended to include portable solar panels, with
     the suggestion that such technology could help reduce energy costs and
     provide longer-term benefits for residents. It was explained that there
     was nothing in the current guidance that specifically prevented portable
     solar panels from being supported through the scheme.
 Members commended all officers involved
     and were proud of this Council in making a difference. 


 

Note:
*Report previously circulated
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve the recommendations for the local delivery of the Crisis and Resilience Fund in Mid Devon.

content:
Cabinet
had before it a report * from the Head of People, Performance and Waste and the
Environment & Enforcement Manager setting out proposals made by the Car Parking
Consultative Group for approval regarding future changes to permit parking
within MDDC car park.

 

The
Cabinet Member for Governance, Finance and Risk outlined the contents of the
report with particular reference to the following: 

 


 It was reported that
     the paper contained the latest recommendations from the Car Parking
     Consultative Group regarding parking and permit arrangements across the
     district.
 A new business parking
     permit was proposed for use in any long-stay car park between the hours of
     6.00am and 6.00pm, at an annual cost of £245.50.
 The proposed permit
     followed the introduction of the new day permit and aimed to provide a
     flexible option for businesses.
 The issue of parking
     accessibility for market traders had been considered in line with
     Cabinet’s earlier direction.
 The free parking for
     market traders was already provided at the Council run markets in Tiverton
     and Cullompton.
 No additional free
     parking measures had been requested by the Consultative Group, although
     future proposals would continue to be considered through the Group and the
     Economy and Assets PDG.


 

Discussion
took place with regards to:

 


 Whether the proposed
     Business Day Permit would be valid for use in only one nominated long-stay
     car park? It was confirmed that was correct.
 Whether the one-day
     permit could it be transferrable between Wellbrook
     Street and Tiverton Multi- Story Car Park? It was confirmed this could be
     supported if Cabinet wished to make a recommendation.
 Whether the Car
     Parking Consultative Group considered extending the day permits to
     Saturday? It had been discussed but nothing had formally been put forward.
     
 Would the permits be
     interchangeable within a business? It was explained that if permit holders
     accessed the portal, they could make those changes as and when needed.
 Could charities with a
     premises apply for a permit and use for their guests? It was confirmed
     this was discussed at Economy and Assets PDG and were advised that
     officers would take information back to the Car Parking Consultative
     Group. 
 If Members wished for
     a permit to be issued for Wellbrook Street could
     it be transferable to the multi-storey car park. Could this restriction be
     capable of operating on the Enforcement Officers machines, or does it have
     to be district wide? It was explained that the permit would be designed
     for the way it was used. 


 

The
Leader MOVED an AMENDMENT

 


 To introduce a new
     type of business permit called a ‘Long Stay Business Permit’. For use
     within all long stay car parks within the District. 


 

Upon
a vote being taken the AMENDMENT was declared to have
been CARRIED.

 

Upon
a vote being taken the MOTION was declared to have been CARRIED.

 

RESOLVED that and APPROVED:

 


 To introduce a new type
     of business permit called a ‘Long Stay Business Permit’. For use within
     all long stay car parks within the district. 


 


 For the ‘Long Stay
     Business Permit’ to be introduced from the 1 April 2027 following the
     necessary statutory public consultation period so it aligned with any
     subsequent proposals regarding parking tariffs. 


 


 The Car Parking
     Consultative Group bring a review paper to the December 2026 meeting of
     the Economy and Assets PDG to review take up of the recently introduced
     day permit which was implemented on the 1 June 2026. 


 


 To maximise the
     accessibility of free parking for market traders to support events across
     the district where appropriate. Future suggestions to be put forward to
     the Car Parking Consultative Group. 
     


 


 On putting forward new
     permit recommendations for consideration by Cabinet, to request that
     Cabinet subsequently grants Delegated Authority to the Director of Legal,
     People & Governance (Monitoring Officer) to draft the order amending
     the Off-Street Parking Places Order (OSPPO) including making the necessary
     required minor amendments to go out to consultation. 


 


 On being satisfied
     that the statutory grounds for amending and varying the OSPPO were met, as
     detailed in the Report, to then allow and authorise the Operations Manager
     for Street Scene and Open Spaces to commence statutory consultation for
     the proposed amendments. 


 


 In the event that
     there were no material objections to the proposed amendments and
     variations as determined by the Operations Manager for Street Scene and
     Open Spaces, in consultation with the Cabinet Member for Finance
     Governance and Risk, to then grant delegated authority to the Director of
     Legal, People and Governance (Monitoring Officer) to make the order
     amending the OSPPO as recommended in the Report.


 

As
recommended by the Economy and Asset Policy Development Group.  

 

(Proposed
by Cllr J Downes and seconded by Cllr J Wright)

 

Reason
for Decision:

This
report aligned with the Corporate Plan to deliver sustainable parking options
within communities. Therefore, supporting economy and growth within the
district.

 

Note:


(i)             
*Report previously circulated

(ii)            
Cllr G Cochran declared he was the Chair of the Car Parking Consultation
Group when this was discussed.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to introduce a new 'Long Stay Business Permit' for all long stay car parks within the district.

Cabinet
had before it a report * from the Head of Revenues, Benefits & Leisure and
the Operations Manager for Leisure presenting the Active Mid Devon Service
Strategy 2026–2030 (the Strategy) for consideration and approval. The Strategy
sets out the strategic direction for the Council’s leisure, sport and wellbeing
services over the next four years, aligning local service delivery with
national active wellbeing priorities, the Council’s Corporate Plan, and the
climate and health agendas.

 

The
Cabinet Member for Service Delivery and Continuous Improvement outlined the
contents of the report with particular reference to
the following: 

 


 The Active Together
     Leisure Strategy 2026–2030 had been developed to support a healthier, more
     active and connected Mid Devon. 
 The strategy focused
     on improving health and wellbeing through increased participation and the
     introduction of Active Communities initiatives. 
 A commitment had been
     made to promote environmental sustainability by reducing carbon emissions
     and improving energy efficiency. 
 Measures were proposed
     to strengthen financial sustainability through increased participation,
     operational efficiencies and new income opportunities. 
 The strategy included
     a programme of digital transformation to enhance customer experience and
     improve service delivery. 
 The strategy adopted
     an active wellbeing approach, working in partnership with organisations
     including the NHS, Active Devon, libraries, community groups and local
     clubs. 
 The Leisure Service
     strategy aimed to maximise existing assets, increase participation and
     ensure the long-term sustainability of leisure services. 
 Success would be
     measured through increased activity levels, membership growth, improved
     health outcomes and greater social value for residents. 
 It was concluded that
     the strategy provided a clear framework for delivering accessible,
     inclusive and sustainable leisure opportunities over the next five years.


 

Discussion
took place with regards to:

 


 Appreciation was
     expressed for the Leisure Strategy, particularly its vision, mission and
     emphasis on community outreach and active wellbeing. 
 Support was given to
     the strategy’s recognition of the wider role Leisure Services played in
     improving health, social connection and community wellbeing. 
 The focus on social
     prescribing and partnership working with GPs and NHS professionals was
     welcomed. 
 A question was raised
     regarding the practical steps already being taken to support and develop
     social prescribing initiatives within Mid Devon. It was confirmed that
     engagement with social prescribers was already in place.
 How would the centre
     differentiate between those people when they presented at the Leisure
     Centres? A report identified those users by postcode which could highlight
     potential opportunities for the future. 
 Whether the Leisure
     Centres requested feedback from General Practice (GP) referrals? It was
     confirmed that they aimed to try and get feedback at the end of the
     referral period.  


 

RESOLVED
that the
‘Leisure Strategy – Active Together’ as recommended by the Service Delivery
& Continuous Improvement Policy Development Group (PDG) be APPROVED.

 

(Proposed
by Cllr J Wright and seconded by Cllr J Downes)

 

Reason
for Decision:

The
Strategy directly supported delivery of the Mid Devon District Council
Corporate Plan 2024–2028 and makes an important contribution to several of its
key priorities, as highlighted in the report.

 

Note:


(i)             
*Report previously circulated

(ii)            
Councillors J Downes, G DuChesne, M Fletcher and J Wright declared that
they were all Members of Active Mid Devon.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve the Active Mid Devon Service Strategy 2026–2030, setting the strategic direction for leisure, sport, and wellbeing services over the next four years.

content:
Amendments
to the Hackney Carriage and Private Hire Policy 2025.



REASON FOR DECISION: 

As per Council decision 30 October 2024 (Item
8(10)); Council approved delegated authority for minor amendments to be made to
the Hackney Carriage and Private Hire Policy 2024 (Taxi Policy) by the Head of
Housing and Health. 

 

This decision records the amendments to be made.

 

Policy changes: 

 

1.    
Introduction of 5 new penalty point categories under the driver and
operator sections: 

 

Following feedback on the initial implementation of
the adopted policy approach to licensed driver point, it was identified that
there would be benefit of some clarity around several existing categories which
can be addressed through more specific descriptions to ensure relevant,
appropriate choices are available.

 

1.1                              
Driver points

 

D50 -       Leaving a Hackney carriage unattended on
a Hackney carriage rank – 3 points 

 

D51 -       Driving in an inconsiderate manner or
below the standard expected of a licenced  driver
– 9 points

 

D52 -       Refusing an in-district fare – 12 points –
prosecutable offence under TPCA1847         level
2 fine applicable

 

D53 -       Driver using an unlicenced vehicle to
fulfil a booking/ journey – 12 points –   prosecutable
offence under S46 LGMP1976 level 3 fine applicable

 

1.2                              
Operator point

 

O38 -       Allowing an unlicenced vehicle to be used
for a booking – 12 points –   prosecutable
offence under S46 LGMP1976 level 3 fine applicable

 

2.    
Removal of paragraph 4.8.4 from policy.

 

Following consultation with
drivers and feedback from licence holders that the DAVIS platform is not adding
value to their experience transacting with the Council, and requested that we
do not require them to use this platform. The key information will be provided
by proprietors directly to the licensing team instead.

 

4.8.4 The Council
provides on online platform for vehicle proprietors to upload details of their
vehicles and associated documents. Instructions on how to access the system are
provided to Licensees on grant of licence. The following documentation can be
submitted through the Davis platform: (a) MOT certificate (b) Insurance
certificate (c) Confirmation of vehicle tax

content:
The
Group had before it and NOTED a report * from the Head of Revenues,
Benefits and Leisure and the Revenues and Benefits Operational Manager
presenting the Crisis, Resilience, Heating Oil Support and Housing Payments
with a forward recommendation to Cabinet to adopt. 

 

The
following was highlighted: 

 

·       It was confirmed that the new government funded Crisis
and Resilience Fund had launched in April 2026. This replaced the previous
discretionary support schemes. The fund encompassed crisis payments, housing
support, resilience services and targeted heating oil assistance to promote a
more cohesive framework. 

·       The fund would be delivered by Devon County Council
(DCC), with local administration by District Councils and partners. 

 

A
discussion took place regarding: 

 

·       The fund would require oversight from Devon County
Council (DCC) and the District Council. It was confirmed that DCC, the
Government and the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) were first-tier
authorities and therefore acted as the ultimate liaison. 

·       The Council had analysed and identified 63 individual
customers who were in receipt of local Council Tax support and relied on oil as
their main source of heating. These customers were invited to attend Churches
Housing Action Team (CHAT) to claim a £400 cash voucher for oil. 

·       The Council operated a general Crisis and Resilience
Fund application process for low-income households or households in receipt of
benefits, whose main source of heating was oil. 

·       It was confirmed that nine customers had received
vouchers totalling approximately £3,500.

·       Councillors received an email confirming the scheme
and were encouraged to discuss the fund with residents.  

·       It was confirmed that the Council had identified a
group of potential eligible oil recipients by reviewing Council Tax reduction
recipients, previous recipients of high energy cost schemes and by comparing
records with Energy Performance Certificate (EPC) data relating to oil heating,
to promote engagement.

·       What was the threshold for low-income households? It
was confirmed that each application would be reviewed on their own merit. 

·       It was confirmed by the DWP that, if the fund was not
spent on oil, then reallocation to the Crisis fund could be considered and vice
versa. 

·       It was confirmed that in paragraph 7.5 of the report
reference was made to £132,630 being added to the current Crisis Fund due to
the significant rise in oil prices. In time, this would become a part of the
settlement. 

·       Are there opportunities for Mid Devon Housing tenants
to covert their energy type? It was confirmed the
Council had programmes in place which supported energy efficiency however, the majority of properties were on gas, air source heat
pumps or electrical systems. 

 

The
Group NOTED the criteria and funding allocations for the new national
scheme.

 

The
Group AGREED to forward the report onto Cabinet for noting. 

 

Proposed
from the Chair. 

 

Note:
Report previously Circulated
topline: The Community, People & Equalities Policy Development Group has decided to adopt a new government funded Crisis, Resilience, Heating Oil Support and Housing Payments scheme.

The
Cabinet had before it a report * from the Head of Finance, Property and Climate
Resilience and the Climate and Sustainability Specialist proposing the approval
of the 2026-28 Climate Action Plan.

 

The
Cabinet Member for Environment and Climate outlined the contents of the report
with particular reference to the following:

 


 Over the past two years the Council continued to
     make progress in reducing the operational carbon footprint, including the
     successful delivery of net zero housing, upgrades to energy efficiency
     across Leisure Centres and the expansion of electric and low emission
     fleet vehicles.
 The draft Climate Action Plan for the next two
     years had built on the achievements and set out the next phase of actions
     to deliver the Council’s climate responsibilities in line with national
     legislation.


 

Discussion
took place with regards to:

 


 Clarification on why the score for the Exe Valley
     gas item in table 2.2.3 changed from zero to minus 50, despite the
     decision not to proceed due to operational constraints. It was explained
     that the table should include in the future, a target emission and
     progress to date and how to read the table.


 

RESOLVED that the draft Climate Action Plan 2026-28, as
recommended by the Planning, Environment and Sustainability Policy Development
Group (PDG), be APPROVED.

 

(Proposed
by Cllr N Bradshaw and seconded by Cllr J Wright)

 

Reason
for Decision:

The
Council’s environmental sustainability duties were underpinned by legislation
e.g. Environment Act 2021. All local authorities had obligations under the
Climate Change Act 2008 with regard to climate change
adaptation (resilience) and mitigation (emission reductions). Full Council had
declared a Climate Emergency in June 2019.

 

Note:
* Report previously circulated.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve the 2026-28 Climate Action Plan, aligning with national legislation and the Council's Climate Emergency declaration.

The Cabinet had before it a
report * from the Head of Housing and Health and the Operations Manager for
Public Health on the award of a contract.

 

The Cabinet Member for
Housing, Assets and Property Services outlined the contents of the report
with particular reference to the following:

 


 The report was to advise Members on the results for the tendering
     of the conversion and renovation of The Laurels, Station Road, Tiverton,
     EX16 4LF (formerly Vale Vets) for the purposes of providing temporary
     homelessness accommodation and agree the award of the contract.
 The Local Authority Housing Fund 3 (LAHF3) funding provided the
     Council with a grant of approximately 50% towards the build/acquisition
     and refurbishment of property for use as dedicated, high-quality temporary
     homelessness accommodation (TA). This built on the Council’s successful
     draw down of funds from the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local
     Government (MHCLG) under the first LAHF round.  
 Due to the nature and value of this procurement, the appropriate
     procedure was an open procurement process. This meant that anyone who
     expressed an interest in the contract would be invited to tender.  
 To ensure quality of contractors, several minimum requirements
     were set out within the Invitation to Tender (ITT).


 

RESOLVED that:

 

1.    
The award of The
Laurels - Temporary Accommodation Project Contract to be awarded to Contractor
6.

 

2.    
Delegated
authority be granted to the S151 Officer (in consultation with the Cabinet
Member for Housing, Assets and Property Services) to complete the associated
The Laurels Temporary Accommodation Project Contract (the Contract).

 

(Proposed by Cllr J Lock and
seconded by Cllr D Wulff)

 

Reason for Decision:

The Council had a legal duty
to maintain the health and safety of its employees and those that occupy
temporary accommodation provided by the Council. The Contract would enable
accommodation units to be delivered in compliance with relevant requirements and
other statutory obligations.

 

Note 

(i)*Report
previously circulated.

(ii) Councillors: N Bradshaw
and J Wright ABSTAINED from voting and G DuChesne voted AGAINST.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to award a contract for the conversion and renovation of a property to provide temporary homelessness accommodation.

The
Cabinet had before it a report * from the Head of Finance, Property and Climate
Resilience and the Climate and Sustainability Specialist providing an update on
the Devon Local Nature Recovery Strategy (LNRS).

 

The
Cabinet Member for Environment and Climate outlined the contents of the report
with particular reference to the following:

 

·      
The LNRS was a
statutory framework that set out local priorities for restoring and enhancing
nature across the County.

·      
Devon’s draft
strategy went through a six-week public consultation last Autumn. This
Council played an active role as the supporting Authority, helping to shape the
content, promote engagement and feedback views from Members, officers and
partners.

·      
The public
response to Devon County Council was overwhelmingly positive demonstrating
strong support for the direction of the strategy and clear appetite locally to
contribute to nature recovery.

·      
The consultation
also had led to a series of improvements to the LNRS including mapping tools,
website usability and clarity of role and made it clear for organisations to
use. 

 

 

RESOLVED that the Local Nature Recovery Strategy as
recommended by the Planning, Environment and Sustainability Policy Development
Group be ENDORSED.

 

(Proposed
by Cllr N Bradshaw and seconded by Cllr G DuChesne)

 

Reason
for Decision:

The
Councils Corporate Plan Priority 1.4: “We will ensure that biodiversity is
increased across the district”. Priority 1.5: “We will value and protect Mid
Devon’s natural and built environment.”

 

Note:
* Report previously circulated.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to endorse the Local Nature Recovery Strategy in Devon.

content:
The Cabinet had before it a
report * from the Director of Place and Economy and the Forward Planning Team
Leader seeking approval to appoint a suitable consultant to prepare an
Anaerobic Guidance.  

 

The Cabinet Member for Planning,
Economic and Regeneration outlined the contents of the report
with particular reference to the following:

 


 The Anaerobic Digestor (AD) Guidance Note would not be a policy
     but would be an informative document that Members and officers could use
     to enable them to be better informed about the operation of AD plants and
     some issues that could arise with them.
 The Guidance Note could potentially inform future policy
     development or guidance if this were considered necessary in the context
     of preparing the Mid Devon Local Plan.
 Officers undertook internet research to check if there was already
     suitable guidance which could be used by this Council.  No
     suitable existing guidance was found.
 Other councils within the County were approached with the
     potential for undertaking a joint commission of this Guidance
     Note.  There was no appetite from other planning authorities to
     jointly commission for this work.
 A procurement process had been undertaken to find a suitable
     consultant to undertake the preparation of the guidance document.


 

Discussion took place with
regards to:

 


 Assurance that the proposed AD Guidance would clearly address
     relevant legal considerations, including indirect and cumulative impacts
     and the concerns from recent AD planning applications would be reflected
     to ensure transparent, robust and legally defensible decision-making. 
 Clarification was requested on how the guidance would align with
     the Corporate Plan 2024–2028, particularly Priority 1.5 on protecting the
     natural and built environment and challenging unmitigated environmental
     harm. It was explained that the specification was set out in the document
     and had regard to the public questions that were raised previously at the
     Council meeting. 
 It was noted that a £12k budget was not considered an efficient or
     proportionate use of funds for producing guidance to inform development
     proposals.


 

RESOLVED that:

 


 Contractor 1 was awarded the contract to prepare an Anaerobic
     Digester Guidance Document.
 Delegated authority be granted to the S151 Officer (in
     consultation with the Cabinet Member for Planning and Economic
     Regeneration and Cabinet Member for Environment and Climate Change) to
     complete the associated Anaerobic Digester Guidance Document Contract. 


 

(Proposed by Cllr D Wulff and
seconded by Cllr N Bradshaw)

 

Reason for Decision:

The Anaerobic Digester
Guidance Document would be capable of being used by the Council to help it
achieve objectives in the Corporate Plan 2024 – 2028.

 

Note *Report previously
circulated.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to award Contractor 1 the contract to prepare an Anaerobic Digester Guidance Document.

Climate and Sustainability Specialist on approving a proposal to establish a Strategic
Sustainability Grant Scheme.

 

The Cabinet Member for
Environment and Climate outlined the contents of the report with particular reference to the following:

 


 The Community-led based initiatives often complemented the
     Council’s own work.
 The scheme was designed to support that strength by helping with
     the co-ordination costs and increasing capacity that other funders did not
     typically cover.
 The proposal set out how the scheme would operate including
     eligibility, funding levels and the intended partnership framework.
 It outlined how the grants would align with the Council’s
     strategic priorities for climate action, nature recovery and wider
     sustainability outcomes.


 

Discussion took place with
regards to:

 


 Whether new or emerging community groups, without an established
     organisational structure, would be eligible to apply where funds were
     administered temporarily through a Town or Parish Council, without being
     formally affiliated to it. It was explained that the fund was primarily
     intended for independent Community Interest companies (CICs), Charitable Incorporated
     Organisations (CIOs) and charities, as Town and Parish Councils could
     raise funds via the precept. Members were requested to promote this
     opportunity through the Town and Parish Council network.


 

RESOLVED that:

 


 The Strategic Sustainability Grant proposal be APPROVED. 


 


 That delegated authority be granted to the Cabinet Member for
     Environment and Climate Change in consultation with Head of Finance,
     Property and Climate Resilience to develop and commence the Strategic
     Sustainability Grant scheme within a specified budget and timeline limits.


 

As recommended by the
Planning, Environment and Sustainability Policy Development Group (PDG).

 

(Proposed by Cllr N Bradshaw
and seconded by Cllr G Duchesne)

 

Reason for Decision:

The Council’s environmental
sustainability duties were underpinned by legislation e.g. Environment Act
2021. All local authorities had obligations under the Climate Change Act 2008 with regard to climate change adaptation (resilience) and
mitigation (emission reductions). 

 

Note: * Report previously
circulated.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve a proposal for a Strategic Sustainability Grant Scheme to support community-led initiatives in alignment with the Council's environmental sustainability duties.

content:
The
Cabinet had before it a report * from the Deputy Chief Executive (S151)
proposing the Council’s revised Asset Management Strategy covering the period 2026
to 2030. The Strategy outlined how the Council would manage its assets,
focusing on a compliance first approach.

 

The
Cabinet Member for Housing, Assets and Property Services outlined the contents
of the report with particular reference to
the following:

 


 The report set out, at a high level, how the
     Council would manage, maintain and invest in their land and property
     assets to support service delivery, financial sustainability, and climate
     objectives. It also aligned asset decisions more closely with the Corporate
     Plan, the Medium‑Term Financial Plan and the net zero ambitions.
 The Strategy covered General Fund assets, not the
     Housing Revenue Accounts (HRA) assets which were covered by a separate
     Strategy. 
 The Strategy placed a clear emphasis on a
     compliance‑first approach, recognising the Councils statutory
     responsibilities as a building owner, employer, landlord and occupier. 
 The property assets were relatively few – with
     approximately12 key operational assets, approximately 60 commercially
     managed assets, and approximately 80 parks and open spaces (including play
     areas). 


 

RESOLVED that the revised Asset Management Strategy for
2026 to 2030 be APPROVED, and delegated approval be given to the Head of
Finance, Property and Climate Resilience to finalise for publication as
recommended by the Economy and Asset Policy Development Group (PDG).

 

(Proposed
by Cllr J Lock and seconded by Cllr N Bradshaw)

 

Reason
for Decision:

Authorities
were required by regulation to have regard to the Prudential Code when carrying
out their duties under Part 1 of the Local Government Act 2003. There were
various statutory or regulatory requirements placed upon the Council as an
owner occupier, landlord and employer. The compliance first approach would
ensure the Council was fully protected.

 

Note:
* Report previously circulated.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve the Council's revised Asset Management Strategy for 2026 to 2030.

content:
The
Cabinet had before it a report * from the Head of Housing and Health on the
Corporate Anti-Social Behaviour Policy providing an update across the district.

 

The
Cabinet Member for Quality of Living, Equalities and Public Health outlined the
contents of the report with particular reference to the following:

 


 The Council was committed to fostering a safe,
     supportive and thriving environment for all who lived, worked and spent
     time in the district. Central to this commitment was ensuring that
     individuals could enjoy their homes and communities free from intimidation,
     harassment and nuisance. 
 Anti-social behaviour (ASB) could significantly
     impact the quality of life of residents and visitors, and addressing it
     effectively was an essential part of the Council’s wider community safety
     responsibilities.
 This report introduced the Council’s updated,
     Corporate Anti-Social Behaviour Policy, which outlined the Council’s
     approach to preventing, managing and resolving ASB in a proportionate,
     fair and victim-centred manner.


 

RESOLVED that the updated, Corporate Anti-Social
Behaviour Policy as attached in Annex A be ADOPTED as recommended by
Community, People and Equalities Policy Development Group.

 

(Proposed
by Cllr D Wulff and seconded by Cllr G DuChesne)

 

Reason
for Decision:

The
Anti-Social Behaviour Policy ensured that the Council operated in full
compliance with the Anti-Social Behaviour, Crime and Policing Act 2014, which
provided the statutory framework for tackling ASB. 

 

Note:
* Report previously circulated.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to adopt the updated Corporate Anti-Social Behaviour Policy to address anti-social behaviour in a fair and victim-centred manner.

content:

and the Corporate Performance and Improvement Manager providing an update on
actions taken to help meet the Council’s statutory duties.

 

The
Cabinet Member for People Development outlined the contents of the report
with particular reference to the following:

 


 The draft Single Equality Scheme for 2026/27 was
     an important document which set out to show that the Council understood
     its communities and detailed what actions would be taken to improve the
     lives of residents.
 Section two of the Single Equality Scheme was the
     Equality Profile for the region. This provided a significant amount of
     data and information which included important insights. This fed into the
     actions that the Council would deliver, articulated through the Equality
     Objectives. These objectives had been reviewed by officers and Members who
     attended the Equality, Diversity and Inclusion Group (EDI) and had been
     further refined for the year ahead.
 Reflecting on the Equality Objectives for the
     last financial year, progress made was provided in the Equality Action
     Plan Report at Appendix 2. 


 

Discussion
took place with regards to:

 


 The opportunities that the Council housing team
     had with engaging their tenant’s involvement and advised Members that the
     Council publish a monthly newsletter.
 The Council to consider an informal allotment
     scheme to encourage residents to grow their own fruit and vegetables. 


 

RESOLVED that the Single Equality Scheme together with
the Equality Objectives for 2026/27 be APPROVED. 

 

As
recommended by the Community, People and Equalities Policy Development Group
(PDG).

 

(Proposed
by Cllr M Fletcher and seconded by Cllr J Lock)

 

Reason
for Decision:

The
Single Equality Scheme contributed to the Council complying with the Equality
Act (2010). Failure to adopt Equality Objectives or to collect relevant data
could lead to the Council being in breach of the Equality Act 2010.

 

Note:
* Report previously circulated.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve the Single Equality Scheme and Equality Objectives for 2026/27 to ensure compliance with the Equality Act (2010).

 The policy applied across all of the Council’s
